extracted.intended_audience: readers of Georgia Straight / general Vancouver arts & culture audience interested in corporate lifestyle news
extracted.subtask_description: A short news-style item reporting and contextualizing controversial remarks by a company founder (quotes, source attribution, clarifications, and reader reaction). Typically appears in a lifestyle/style section of a local/online paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Byline and timestamp
rubrics_metrics.description: Include the author's name and the publication date/time prominently on the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This page shows 'by Michelle da Silva on November 6th, 2013 at 4:35 PM' — include clear attribution so readers know who wrote the piece and when it ran.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section/category labeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Label the article under a section or category to signal tone and topical focus (e.g., Style).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article is presented under 'Style' — using a section label helps readers place the story in context (arts/culture/lifestyle vs. business/news).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use direct quotations with clear attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Quote speakers verbatim where possible and attribute those quotes to the interview medium and interviewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece reproduces direct quotes from Chip Wilson and attributes them to 'Bloomberg TV' and 'Bloomberg TV's Trish Regan' (e.g., 'There has always been pilling... some women’s bodies just don’t work for it'). Always identify who said what and where the remarks were made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide clarifying context and alternative perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Include immediate clarifications or qualifying remarks from other participants or relevant actors when a quoted statement could be ambiguous or controversial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article records Shannon Wilson's clarification ('it was more about what activities customers are doing') and Chip Wilson's further clarification ('I just think it's how you use them'). Including such context helps readers understand intent and reduces misinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link to related information and follow-up facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide links or short mentions of relevant follow-up facts, related stories, or background details that help readers understand broader implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The story notes the company 'is still on the hunt for a new CEO' and links the phrase 'new CEO' — linking to related coverage/background helps readers explore the issue further.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concise headline capturing the controversy
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a clear, attention-getting headline that summarizes the central claim or controversy of the piece.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Headline example from the page: 'Chip Wilson blames women's bodies for lululemon complaints' — the headline frames the key dispute succinctly for quick reader comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide author contact / social links
rubrics_metrics.description: Offer a way for readers to follow or contact the author (e.g., social media handle).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article includes 'You can follow Michelle da Silva on Twitter at twitter.com/michdas' — adding such links encourages engagement and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present reader reaction via comments with metadata
rubrics_metrics.description: Host a comments section that displays usernames, timestamps, comment text, and community ratings/counts to surface public response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This page includes comments with names, timestamps, comment body, 'Rating:' display, and counts (e.g., '31 Comments', individual comment ratings). Presenting comments and ratings gives readers a sense of public sentiment and fosters discussion.
